subject: Mathematics
title: Rohan's Tile Shop: Squares and Cubes
hook: How does a tile shop owner calculate orders using perfect squares and cubes?

slides.title: A Square and A Cube
slides.storyContext: Rohan's tile shop needs to order ceramic tiles. His supplier charges by square meter for floor tiles and by cubic meter for storage boxes. Priya watches as Kumar Uncle teaches the math behind the order.

image.alt: A Square and A Cube — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: The Order Problem
slides.storyContext: A customer wants a 6 meter × 6 meter bathroom floor covered with 1 meter × 1 meter tiles. Rohan calculates: 6 × 6 = 36 tiles. But the supplier lists the area as "6 squared." Priya asks: what does that mean?

image.alt: The Order Problem — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Perfect Squares: Numbers That Multiply Themselves

points.label: Definition
points.text: When a number multiplies by itself, the result is a perfect square. If n × n = n², then n² is a perfect square.

example.problem: Rohan's customer has a square courtyard with side 7 meters. How many square meter tiles does he need?
example.solution: Area = 7 × 7 = 7² = 49 square meters. He needs 49 tiles.

slides.inSimpleWords: A perfect square is the result when you multiply a number by itself. 5 × 5 = 25, so 25 is a perfect square.

image.alt: Perfect Squares: Numbers That Multiply Themselves — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Finding Square Roots: Reversing Multiplication

points.label: Definition
points.text: The square root of a number n (written √n) is the number you multiply by itself to get n. If m² = n, then √n = m.

points.label: Real-world use
points.text: If Rohan knows he needs exactly 81 tiles to cover a square floor, he can find the side: √81 = 9 meters.

example.problem: A square kitchen has area 144 square meters. What is the side length?
example.solution: Side length = √144 = 12 meters (because 12 × 12 = 144).

slides.inSimpleWords: The square root reverses squaring. If 9² = 81, then √81 = 9.

image.alt: Finding Square Roots: Reversing Multiplication — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Perfect Cubes: Volume in Three Dimensions

points.label: Definition
points.text: When a number multiplies by itself THREE times, the result is a perfect cube. If n × n × n = n³, then n³ is a perfect cube.

points.label: Real-world use
points.text: Rohan stores tiles in cubic boxes. A box with side 3 meters holds 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic meters of tiles.

example.problem: A storage room is a perfect cube with side 5 meters. What is its volume?
example.solution: Volume = 5 × 5 × 5 = 5³ = 125 cubic meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: A perfect cube is the result when you multiply a number by itself three times. 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, so 64 is a perfect cube.

image.alt: Perfect Cubes: Volume in Three Dimensions — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Common Perfect Squares and Cubes

example.problem: Is 144 a perfect square? Is 125 a perfect cube?

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorizing the first 10–15 perfect squares and cubes helps you solve problems faster without a calculator.

image.alt: Common Perfect Squares and Cubes — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Recognizing Non-Perfect Squares and Cubes

points.label: Not every number is perfect
points.text: Numbers like 50, 100 (perfect), 127 (not perfect), etc. Some are perfect, many are not.

points.label: How to check
points.text: Try multiplying candidates. For 50: 7 × 7 = 49, 8 × 8 = 64. Since 49 < 50 < 64, 50 is not a perfect square.

example.problem: Is 48 a perfect cube?
example.solution: Try: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. Since 27 < 48 < 64, 48 is not a perfect cube.

slides.inSimpleWords: If no whole number multiplied by itself (or itself three times) equals your target, then the target is not a perfect square (or cube).

image.alt: Recognizing Non-Perfect Squares and Cubes — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Rohan's Final Order
slides.storyContext: Rohan receives a big order: customer needs 10 square meters of floor tiles (10 different 1m×1m designs) and a storage box with side 4 meters for leftover stock.

example.problem: How many cubic meters does the storage box hold?
example.solution: Volume of box = 4 × 4 × 4 = 4³ = 64 cubic meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares measure area (2D), cubes measure volume (3D). Rohan uses both for his business.

image.alt: Rohan's Final Order — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Your Turn: The Garden Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya's school is building a square vegetable garden with side 8 meters, and a cube-shaped rainwater tank with side 2 meters.

example.problem: Find the garden area and tank volume.
example.solution: Garden area = 8² = 64 square meters. Tank volume = 2³ = 8 cubic meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Remember: squares use ², cubes use ³.

image.alt: Your Turn: The Garden Problem — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A perfect square is n × n = n². Examples: 25 = 5², 100 = 10².
A square root (√n) reverses squaring. √25 = 5.
A perfect cube is n × n × n = n³. Examples: 8 = 2³, 125 = 5³.
Squares measure area (floors, tiles). Cubes measure volume (boxes, tanks).

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares and cubes help us calculate areas and volumes in real life.

image.alt: What We Learned — A Square and A Cube

subject: Mathematics
title: Divya's Number Hunt: Rational and Irrational
hook: Are all numbers fractions? Divya discovers the mystery of numbers that cannot be written as fractions.

slides.title: A Story of Numbers
slides.storyContext: Divya and Anand visit Ms. Sharma's class for a special lesson on numbers. Ms. Sharma asks: "Can every number be written as a fraction?" The answer surprises them.

slides.title: The Fraction Question
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma draws numbers on the board: 1/2, 3, -5, 7/4. Then she asks, "Can you write 3 as a fraction?" Anand says, "Yes! 3 = 3/1." Ms. Sharma smiles and says, "Good. But what about √2? Can you write that as a fraction?" The class goes silent.

image.alt: The Fraction Question — A Story of Numbers

slides.title: Rational Numbers: Fractions We Can Write

points.label: Definition
points.text: A rational number is any number that can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.

example.problem: Is 2.5 a rational number?
example.solution: Yes. 2.5 = 25/10 = 5/2. Since it can be written as a fraction of two integers, it is rational.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rational numbers are any numbers you can write as a fraction: whole numbers, decimals that stop, and repeating decimals.

image.alt: Rational Numbers: Fractions We Can Write — A Story of Numbers

slides.title: Repeating Decimals Are Rational

points.label: Repeating decimals
points.text: Decimals like 0.333... (1/3) and 0.1666... (1/6) repeat forever but are still rational because they equal a fraction.

points.label: How to identify
points.text: If a decimal repeats the same digit or pattern endlessly, it is rational. Example: 0.123123123... repeats "123."

example.problem: Is 0.333... rational?
example.solution: Yes. 0.333... = 1/3. It repeats but equals a fraction, so it is rational.

slides.inSimpleWords: Any decimal that repeats, no matter how long the pattern, can be written as a fraction.

slides.title: Irrational Numbers: Beyond Fractions

points.label: Definition
points.text: An irrational number CANNOT be written as p/q. Its decimal never stops and never repeats.

points.label: Famous examples
points.text: √2 ≈ 1.41421356..., π ≈ 3.14159265..., e ≈ 2.71828... These decimals go on forever with no repeating pattern.

example.problem: Is √2 rational or irrational?
example.solution: Irrational. √2 ≈ 1.414213562... Its decimal never ends and never repeats. It cannot be written as a fraction p/q.

slides.inSimpleWords: Irrational numbers are decimals that go on forever without repeating. You cannot write them as fractions.

image.alt: Irrational Numbers: Beyond Fractions — A Story of Numbers

slides.title: Square Roots and Irrational Numbers

points.label: Perfect squares
points.text: √1 = 1, √4 = 2, √9 = 3, √16 = 4, √25 = 5. These are all rational (integers).

points.label: Non-perfect squares
points.text: √2, √3, √5, √6, √7, √8, √10 are all irrational. Their decimals never end.

example.problem: Which is rational and which is irrational: √25 or √26?
example.solution: √25 = 5 (rational). √26 ≈ 5.099... (irrational—decimal never ends).

slides.inSimpleWords: Square roots of perfect squares are rational. Square roots of non-perfect squares are irrational.

slides.title: Real Numbers: The Complete Number Line

points.label: Definition
points.text: The set of all rational and irrational numbers together is called the real numbers. Every point on the number line is a real number.

points.label: Order
points.text: Real numbers include: negative integers, zero, positive integers, fractions, and irrationals. They can be ordered from smallest to largest.

example.problem: Order these from smallest to largest: -2, 1/2, √2, 3.

slides.inSimpleWords: The real number line contains all numbers—fractions, whole numbers, and never-ending decimals. Together, they form the complete real numbers.

slides.title: Ms. Sharma's Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma asks Divya and Anand to classify 10 numbers. They work together to sort them into rational and irrational.

example.problem: Is π irrational?
example.solution: Yes. π ≈ 3.141592653... Its decimal never ends and never repeats. π cannot be written as p/q.

slides.inSimpleWords: π is irrational because its decimal never terminates or repeats.

slides.title: Your Turn: Classify the Numbers
slides.storyContext: Divya and Anand give you a list: 7, 0.5, √9, √10, 22/7, π. Sort them into rational and irrational.

example.problem: Which are rational and which are irrational?

slides.inSimpleWords: Remember: if it can be written as a fraction, it is rational. If it cannot, it is irrational.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Rational numbers can be written as fractions p/q. Examples: 1/2, 3, 2.5, 0.333...
Irrational numbers cannot be written as fractions. Their decimals never end and never repeat. Examples: √2, π, e.
Real numbers include all rational and irrational numbers.
Square roots of perfect squares are rational; square roots of non-perfect squares are irrational.

slides.inSimpleWords: Not all numbers are fractions. Some numbers, like √2 and π, are irrational and cannot be written as fractions.

image.alt: What We Learned — A Story of Numbers

subject: Mathematics
title: Vikram's Sweet Shop: Expanding Expressions
hook: When Vikram distributes sweets to groups, the numbers multiply in unexpected ways. Learn the algebra of expansion.

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: school friend learning algebra from Vikram

slides.title: We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply
slides.storyContext: Vikram's sweet shop receives bulk orders. He uses algebra to calculate: if each customer wants (a + b) sweets from c different vendors, how many total? His method: distribute, then multiply.

slides.title: The Festival Order
slides.storyContext: A school festival orders sweets. Vikram knows: each of the 3 booths gets 2 types of sweets (gulab jamun and laddu). So each booth wants (2 + 3) sweets... wait, he realizes it's (g + l) where g = gulab jamun, l = laddu. When 5 shopkeepers each order the same mix (g + l), the total is 5(g + l). But how many sweets is that?

image.alt: The Festival Order — We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply

slides.title: The Distributive Property: Multiply First, Then Add

points.label: Rule
points.text: a(b + c) = ab + ac. When you multiply a number outside brackets by the terms inside, multiply the outside number by EACH term inside.

points.label: Why?
points.text: Imagine 3 bags, each with (2 apples + 4 oranges). Total apples = 3 × 2 = 6. Total oranges = 3 × 4 = 12. Total fruit = 6 + 12 = 18. So 3(2 + 4) = 6 + 12.

example.problem: Expand 5(g + l) where g = gulab jamun, l = laddu.
example.solution: 5(g + l) = 5g + 5l. If each sweet costs the same, Vikram counts: 5 gulab jamun and 5 laddu.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you see a number outside brackets, multiply that number by EVERY term inside the brackets.

slides.title: Expanding with Subtraction

points.label: Rule
points.text: a(b - c) = ab - ac. The distributive property works the same with subtraction.

points.label: Examples
points.text: 3(x - 2) = 3x - 6. If a shop sells (price - discount), and you buy 3, you pay 3price - 3discount.

example.problem: A customer buys 4 boxes. Each box has (x chocolates - 2 damaged). How many good chocolates total?
example.solution: 4(x - 2) = 4x - 8 good chocolates.

slides.inSimpleWords: Subtraction in brackets: multiply the outside number by each term, and keep the minus sign.

image.alt: Expanding with Subtraction — We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply

slides.title: Expanding Two Brackets: (a + b)(c + d)

points.label: Rule
points.text: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. Multiply EVERY term in the first bracket by EVERY term in the second.

points.label: Method (FOIL)
points.text: First: a × c. Outer: a × d. Inner: b × c. Last: b × d. Then add all four.

example.problem: Vikram arranges sweets in (x + 3) rows and (y + 2) columns. How many sweets total?

slides.inSimpleWords: When multiplying two brackets, each term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second. You get four products; add them all.

image.alt: Expanding Two Brackets: (a + b)(c + d) — We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply

slides.title: Perfect Square Expansion: (a + b)² and (a - b)²

points.label: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
points.text: Example: (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9.

points.label: (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b²
points.text: Example: (x - 2)² = x² - 4x + 4.

example.problem: A square sweet box has side (a + 5). What is its area?
example.solution: Area = (a + 5)² = a² + 10a + 25 square units.

slides.inSimpleWords: For (a + b)²: square the first term, double the product, then square the second term. (a - b)² is the same but the middle term is negative.

slides.title: Difference of Squares: (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b²

points.label: Rule
points.text: (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b². When the same terms add in one bracket and subtract in the other, the middle cancels.

points.label: Quick factoring
points.text: If you see a² - b², it factors as (a + b)(a - b). Useful for checking work and simplifying.

example.problem: Expand (x + 4)(x - 4).
example.solution: (x + 4)(x - 4) = x² - 16. Notice: no middle term! The +4x and -4x cancel.

slides.inSimpleWords: When two brackets have the same terms but opposite signs (one + one -), multiply to get: (first term)² - (second term)².

slides.title: Vikram's Real Order
slides.storyContext: A restaurant orders sweets in (2x + 3) boxes of (x + 2) sweets each. Vikram must calculate the total.

example.problem: Find the total number of sweets in (2x + 3)(x + 2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Expand by multiplying every term in the first bracket by every term in the second, then combine like terms.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Sweet Box Problem
slides.storyContext: Maya designs a box with dimensions (a + 5) by (a + 5) by (a + 3). What is the volume?

example.problem: Find the volume of a box with dimensions (a + 5) × (a + 5) × (a + 3).
example.solution: First, (a + 5)² = a² + 10a + 25. Then multiply by (a + 3): (a² + 10a + 25)(a + 3) = a³ + 3a² + 10a² + 30a + 25a + 75 = a³ + 13a² + 55a + 75.

slides.inSimpleWords: Expand step by step: first expand the square, then multiply the result by the third dimension.

image.alt: Your Turn: The Sweet Box Problem — We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Distributive property: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
Expanding two brackets: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd.
Perfect squares: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b².
Difference of squares: (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b².

slides.inSimpleWords: Expanding means removing brackets by multiplying and adding terms. Master these patterns to simplify algebra.
